problem.text: A number $m$ is randomly selected from the set $\{11, 13, 15, 17, 19\}$, and a number $n$ is randomly selected from $\{1999, 2000, 2001, \ldots, 2018\}$. What is the probability that $m^n$ has a units digit of $1$?

steps.title: Where to start: only the units digit of $m$ matters
steps.body: The question asks only about the units digit of $m^n$, and the units digit of a product depends only on the units digits of the factors. So we can replace $m$ by its units digit: $1, 3, 5, 7$ or $9$. Then count the pairs $(m, n)$ that work, out of all equally likely pairs.

your_turn.prompt: How many values can $n$ take, and how many pairs $(m, n)$ are there in total?

steps.title: The easy digits: 1 and 5
steps.body: A number ending in $1$ always gives a power ending in $1$, so $m = 11$ works for all $20$ values of $n$. A number ending in $5$ always gives a power ending in $5$.

your_turn.prompt: How many values of $n$ work for $m = 15$?

steps.title: Digits 3 and 7 repeat every 4
steps.body: The units digits of $3^1, 3^2, 3^3, 3^4, \ldots$ are $3, 9, 7, 1$ and then repeat. For $7$ they are $7, 9, 3, 1$ and repeat. So $13^n$ and $17^n$ end in $1$ exactly when $n$ is a multiple of $4$.

your_turn.prompt: How many multiples of $4$ are in $\{1999, \ldots, 2018\}$?
your_turn.answer: Five: $2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016$. So $m = 13$ and $m = 17$ each give $5$ good values of $n$.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Careful with $9$: its powers end in $9, 1, 9, 1, \ldots$, a cycle of length $2$, not $4$. So $19^n$ ends in $1$ for every even $n$, and there are $10$ even numbers from $2000$ to $2018$. The total is $20 + 5 + 0 + 5 + 10 = 40$ good pairs out of $100$, so the probability is $\frac{40}{100} = \frac{2}{5}$. The answer is **(E)**.

wrong_choices.D: This comes from treating $9$ like $3$ and $7$ and counting only the $5$ multiples of $4$. But $9^2 = 81$ already ends in $1$, so every even exponent works, giving $10$ values and $40$ good pairs instead of $35$.
